title: Should University Be Free? Two Students Debate

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: I've been thinking a lot about the university fees debate. I really believe that higher education should be free for everyone. It's a fundamental right, not a privilege.

dialogue.speaker: Tomás
dialogue.text: I understand that argument, but I'm not convinced. Who pays for it? If universities are free, the costs fall on taxpayers — including people who never went to university and earn less than graduates.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: That's true, but graduates typically earn significantly more over their lifetimes. So they contribute more in taxes. The system balances itself out eventually.

dialogue.speaker: Tomás
dialogue.text: Eventually is doing a lot of work in that sentence. In the meantime, working-class people are subsidising the education of students who often come from relatively comfortable backgrounds.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: That's exactly why the current system is broken. Rich families can afford fees easily; poorer students graduate with enormous debt. That's not equality of opportunity — it's reinforcing inequality.

dialogue.speaker: Tomás
dialogue.text: But means-tested grants and scholarships can address that. You don't need to make the whole system free. Target the support at those who actually need it.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Means-tested systems are complicated and stigmatising. Many students who are eligible don't apply because of the bureaucracy or the shame. A universal system removes those barriers.

dialogue.speaker: Tomás
dialogue.text: That's a fair point about stigma. But there's another issue: if university is free, demand will increase enormously. Does that mean building more universities? Hiring more lecturers? Where does the money come from?

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: From higher taxes on corporations and the wealthy. Countries like Germany and Norway have free or heavily subsidised higher education. It's not impossible — it's a question of political will and priorities.

dialogue.speaker: Tomás
dialogue.text: Germany has a very different tax culture and economic structure from countries that don't have free university. You can't just copy a system without considering context.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: Fair enough — context matters. But the principle remains: education should not be determined by your parents' bank account. The current situation is a barrier to social mobility.

dialogue.speaker: Tomás
dialogue.text: I agree on the social mobility point. But I think the debate is really about how to fund it fairly, not whether to fund it. On that, we might actually agree more than we think.

dialogue.speaker: Aisha
dialogue.text: That's probably right. The goal is the same — broader access to education. We just disagree on the mechanism.

vocab.definition: to support something financially by paying part of its costs

vocab.definition: a mark of shame or disgrace associated with a particular circumstance
vocab.example: "Means-tested systems are stigmatising — students feel ashamed to apply."

vocab.definition: a system with complex official rules and processes
vocab.example: "Many students don't apply because of the bureaucracy."
